directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Chardonnay needs a long, warm growing season and consistent trellising and pruning to ripen fruit and produce quality wine grapes. The most widely planted white wine grape in the world, it produces tight clusters of small, thin-skinned green-gold grapes that adapt to a remarkably wide range of climates and winemaking styles, from crisp, mineral, unoaked wines in cool regions to rich, buttery, oak-aged wines in warmer ones. Vigorous and relatively easy to grow compared to some finicky wine varieties, it still requires careful canopy management, disease monitoring, and a well-drained site to reach commercial fruit quality, and benefits from professional pruning guidance for home vineyard growers new to viticulture. Train young vines to a permanent trellis system, thin fruit clusters if overcropping occurs, and harvest based on sugar and acid balance rather than a fixed calendar date, since ripeness timing varies significantly by site and season.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Pinot Noir prefers cooler growing regions and is notoriously demanding, susceptible to fungal disease and sensitive to heat and site conditions. One of the world's most celebrated but challenging red wine grapes, it produces thin-skinned, tightly clustered grapes prone to rot in humid or wet conditions, making it best suited to cooler, drier climates with good air circulation rather than hot, humid regions like the Gulf South. Its thin skins and tight clusters demand vigilant canopy management, leaf pulling for airflow, and prompt disease treatment, and it is generally considered one of the more difficult grape varieties for a home vineyard to grow successfully compared to more disease-resistant hybrid grapes. Site vines on a well-drained slope with good air movement, prune for an open canopy to reduce humidity around the fruit, and monitor closely for powdery and downy mildew through the growing season.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Riesling is one of the more cold-hardy classic wine grapes and performs well in cooler climates unsuited to many other vinifera varieties.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Riesling is one of the more cold-hardy classic wine grapes and performs well in cooler climates unsuited to many other vinifera varieties. Late-ripening, aromatic, and capable of producing wines ranging from bone-dry to intensely sweet depending on when the grapes are picked, it retains bright, food-friendly acidity even at high sugar levels, a hallmark that has made it one of the most versatile and food-pairing-friendly white wine grapes grown worldwide. Its relatively high tolerance for winter cold makes it a realistic choice for home vineyards in cooler regions where more tender vinifera varieties struggle to survive, though it still needs a long growing season to fully ripen. Prune for an open canopy to promote airflow and reduce disease pressure, and consider harvest timing carefully, since flavor and sweetness profile change significantly the longer fruit hangs on the vine.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Zinfandel thrives in warm climates and is prone to uneven ripening within a single cluster, requiring careful harvest timing. Genetically identical to the Croatian variety Crljenak Kaštelanski and Italy's Primitivo, this vigorous red wine grape produces loose clusters of thin-skinned, sweet grapes that ripen unevenly on the same bunch, with green, pink, and fully ripe purple-black berries sometimes present simultaneously, a quirk growers must manage carefully to avoid overripe, raisined fruit alongside underripe berries at harvest. Vigorous and productive in warm, sunny climates, it also produces the pink blush wine known as White Zinfandel when pressed with minimal skin contact, making a single variety the source of two very different wine styles. Manage canopy density to promote even ripening, monitor clusters closely as harvest approaches given the variety's uneven ripening tendency, and provide full sun and heat for the best sugar development.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

A cross between Honeycrisp and Enterprise developed by Washington State University and released commercially in 2019 after two decades of breeding and testing, it combines Honeycrisp's exceptionally crisp, juicy texture with dramatically better storage life, keeping fresh in refrigeration for up to a year without the bruising and softening problems that plague its Honeycrisp parent. Large, deep red fruit with a name inspired by the pale lenticel dots scattered across the skin like stars against a dark sky, it has rapidly become one of the most sought-after new apple varieties for both commercial orchards and home growers wanting Honeycrisp's texture without its notorious storage and growing difficulties. Thin fruit in early summer for larger apples, provide a compatible pollinator variety within range, and harvest based on color and taste rather than a fixed date, since ripening time varies by climate.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Envy requires a moderate chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. A New Zealand-bred cross between Braeburn and Royal Gala, it produces large, brilliantly two-toned red-and-pink fruit with dense, sweet, exceptionally slow-to-brown flesh that stays fresh-looking far longer than most apples once cut, making it a favorite for lunchboxes, fruit trays, and salads. The tree is vigorous and productive with good disease resistance for a modern apple, and the fruit's slow browning and long storage life have made it an increasingly popular commercial and home-orchard variety since its introduction. Thin fruit clusters in early summer to improve size and annual bearing, provide a compatible pollinator, and harvest when the background color shifts from green to yellow-green beneath the red blush.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Jazz requires a moderate chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. A New Zealand-bred cross between Gala and Braeburn, it produces medium-sized, densely crisp, juicy fruit with a distinctive sweet-tart flavor balance and a pear-drop aroma that sets it apart from its sweeter Gala parent, marketed commercially since the early 2000s as a premium eating apple. The tree bears reliably and the fruit stores exceptionally well in refrigeration, holding its crisp texture and flavor for months, which has helped make it a popular choice for both commercial orchards and home growers wanting a long-keeping late-season apple. Thin fruit clusters in early summer, provide a compatible pollinator variety, and harvest once the background color turns from green to yellow beneath the red blush for the best flavor balance.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Ambrosia requires a moderate chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. Discovered as a chance seedling in a British Columbia orchard in the 1980s, likely a natural cross of Golden Delicious and Jonagold, it produces large, blushed pink-and-gold fruit with exceptionally low acidity, a honeyed sweetness, and fine, crisp, low-tannin flesh that resists browning better than many apples once cut. The tree is precocious and productive, often bearing at a young age, and the fruit's mild, sweet flavor and attractive coloring have made it a fast-growing favorite in both commercial orchards and home gardens since its introduction. Thin fruit clusters in early summer for larger apples, provide a compatible pollinator, and harvest when the background skin color shifts from green to yellow beneath the pink blush.
sources: British Columbia Ministry of Agriculture reference

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Opal requires a moderate chill period, good disease resistance for a modern apple, and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Opal requires a moderate chill period, good disease resistance for a modern apple, and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. A Czech-bred cross between Golden Delicious and the scab-resistant Topaz, it produces smooth, bright golden-yellow fruit with dense, crisp, exceptionally slow-browning flesh and a sweet, mild flavor, marketed since the 2010s as a naturally non-browning apple achieved through conventional breeding rather than genetic modification. The tree carries good genetic resistance to apple scab, a significant fungal disease that plagues many apple varieties, reducing the need for fungicide spraying in a home orchard setting. Thin fruit clusters in early summer, provide a compatible pollinator variety, and harvest once fruit reaches full golden-yellow color for the best sweetness and texture.
